---
title: "Protein Structure Embeddings"
---

A protein is not a string; it is a physical object that folds into a specific
three-dimensional shape, and that shape is what performs catalysis, binds
partners, and transmits signals. Sequence embeddings (Chapter 5) capture
evolutionary and functional regularities, but they are one projection of the
same underlying object. This chapter treats the complementary projection: how a
protein's 3D structure is turned into a fixed-length vector, and what
guarantees those vectors must satisfy before they can be useful.

The central difficulty is that structure is a *set of points in space*, not a
sequence with a canonical order. Any representation of geometry must therefore
be immune to arbitrary choices of coordinate system. Getting this right — or
wrong — determines whether a model learns shape or memorizes noise.

# Representing Protein Structure

A structure is most directly a table of Cartesian coordinates, one per atom, as
deposited in the Protein Data Bank or predicted by a folding model such as
AlphaFold2 [@jumper2021highly]. Downstream representations almost never consume
raw coordinates directly; they consume derived objects that encode the same
geometry in a form more amenable to learning.

## Coordinates

Let $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$ denote the position of atom (or residue)
$i$ for $i = 1, \dots, N$, and let $\mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}$ be the
coordinate matrix whose $i$-th row is $\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}$. Raw coordinates are
the most information-rich object, but they are also the most fragile: applying a
rigid motion — a rotation $\mathbf{R} \in SO(3)$ (so that
$\mathbf{R}^{\top}\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}$ and $\det \mathbf{R} = +1$) and a
translation $\mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ — sends
$\mathbf{x}_i \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}_i + \mathbf{t}$ and so changes every
coordinate without changing the molecule. A model that reads raw $\mathbf{x}_i$
therefore sees two different inputs for the same structure, which is exactly the
redundancy that invariance is meant to remove.

## Distance matrices and contact maps

A rotation- and translation-invariant description is the **distance matrix**
$D \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$,

$$ D_{ij} = \lVert \mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j \rVert_2, \qquad i, j = 1, \dots, N $$ {#eq-ch06-distance-matrix}

where $\lVert \cdot \rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm (Appendix A). Its entries are
invariant under any rigid motion: substituting
$\mathbf{x}_i \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}_i + \mathbf{t}$ and
$\mathbf{x}_j \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{t}$ gives

$$ \lVert (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}_i + \mathbf{t}) - (\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{t}) \rVert_2 = \lVert \mathbf{R}(\mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j) \rVert_2 = \lVert \mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j \rVert_2 $$ {#eq-ch06-distance-invariance}

because the translation cancels and rotations preserve length,
$\lVert \mathbf{R}\mathbf{y} \rVert_2 = \lVert \mathbf{y} \rVert_2$ (since
$\mathbf{R}^{\top}\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}$). The distance matrix therefore
depends only on intrinsic geometry, not on the coordinate frame in which the
structure happens to be expressed.

A coarser relative is the **contact map** $C \in \{0,1\}^{N \times N}$,

$$ C_{ij} = \mathbb{1}[\,D_{ij} < \tau\,] $$ {#eq-ch06-contact-map}

where $\mathbb{1}[\cdot]$ is the indicator function (1 when the condition holds,
0 otherwise) and $\tau > 0$ is a distance threshold (commonly
$\tau \approx 8\,\text{\AA}$ for heavy-atom contacts). Because $C$ is a
deterministic function of $D$, the contact map of (@eq-ch06-contact-map)
inherits the invariance in (@eq-ch06-distance-invariance). It discards most
of the metrical detail but is compact and robust, and was the standard input to
early residue-contact predictors.

Distances are not perfectly lossless: mirror images share the same distance
matrix but are distinct molecules. Adding chirality-sensitive features (dihedral
angles, or the signed orientation of bonded frames) resolves this.

## Graphs

The most common modern view is a graph on residues, where node $i$ carries
features (amino-acid identity, secondary structure, a learned embedding) and
edges encode proximity. Edges are typically drawn between the $k$ nearest
neighbors in 3D, between sequence neighbors, or within a radius. Edge features
are made invariant by storing distances rather than displacement vectors, and
node updates follow the message-passing template of Gilmer et al.
[@gilmer2017neural]: each node's new state is a learned function of its current
state and the states of its neighbors. The conversion from coordinates to a
residue graph is the pivotal modelling decision of the whole chapter, and is
summarized in @fig-coord-graph.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
A **graph representation** of a protein structure is a tuple
$(\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$ with node features and edge features. **Node
features** describe individual residues; **edge features** describe relationships
between residues and are built to be invariant under rigid motions (for example,
distances). A **geometric** graph neural network is one whose node or edge
features additionally carry rotation-sensitive quantities such as directions.
:::

Formally, write the residue graph as $G = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$ with vertex
set $\mathcal{V} = \{1, \dots, N\}$, edge set
$\mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{V} \times \mathcal{V}$, node features
$\mathbf{h}_i^{(0)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_h}$, and edge features
$\mathbf{e}_{ij} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_e}$. Edges are constructed from the geometry,
for example by radius or by $k$-nearest neighbors,

$$ (i, j) \in \mathcal{E} \iff D_{ij} \le r \ \ \text{or} \ \ j \in \operatorname{kNN}(i) $$ {#eq-ch06-graph}

where $r > 0$ is a radius, $\operatorname{kNN}(i)$ is the set of $k$ indices
nearest to $i$ under $D$, and $D$ is the distance matrix of (@eq-ch06-distance-matrix). Because both criteria in (@eq-ch06-graph) are
functions of $D$ alone, the edge set is also invariant under rigid motion.

The graph view makes the **permutation** symmetry explicit. Stack the node
features into $\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d_h}$; relabelling the residues
by a permutation $\pi$ acts as $\mathbf{H} \mapsto \boldsymbol{\Pi}\mathbf{H}$,
where $\boldsymbol{\Pi} \in \{0,1\}^{N \times N}$ is the permutation matrix with
$\Pi_{\pi(i), i} = 1$ and $\boldsymbol{\Pi}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\Pi} = \mathbf{I}$.
A graph encoder that aggregates over neighbors with a permutation-invariant
operator and pools with a permutation-invariant readout $R$ satisfies

$$ R\big(\{\mathbf{h}_{\pi(i)}\}_{i \in \mathcal{V}}\big) = R\big(\{\mathbf{h}_i\}_{i \in \mathcal{V}}\big) \quad \text{for every permutation } \pi $$ {#eq-ch06-permutation-invariance}

so its output is a function of the *set* of residues, not of the arbitrary index
order in which they were listed. This is why a distance matrix, which is
order-dependent as an array, and a graph, which is order-agnostic, can encode the
same geometry.

```python
# Coordinate tensor vs. graph representation (illustrative)
import numpy as np

coords = np.load("residue_ca.npy")          # (N, 3) Cartesian coordinates
D = np.linalg.norm(coords[:, None] - coords[None], axis=-1)   # (N, N) distances
k = 10
knn = np.argsort(D, axis=1)[:, 1:k + 1]     # (N, k) nearest neighbors
edge_index = np.stack([np.repeat(np.arange(len(coords)), k), knn.reshape(-1)])
```

::: {#fig-coord-graph}
*Coordinate versus graph representations.* Left: a protein is a cloud of points
$\mathbf{x}_i$ together with edges; the coordinates change under rotation and
translation while the graph and its distance edge features do not. Right: the
same structure is encoded either as a distance/contact matrix (an $N \times N$
array, order-dependent) or as a residue graph (node features plus an edge list,
order-agnostic). The graph formulation is what GNN-based structure encoders
consume.
:::

# Invariance and Equivariance

The vocabulary that makes the above precise is invariance and equivariance.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
Let $f$ be a function on structures and let $g \cdot x$ be the action of a
transformation $g$ (rotation, translation, or node permutation). Then $f$ is
**invariant** if $f(g \cdot x) = f(x)$, and **equivariant** if
$f(g \cdot x) = g \cdot f(x)$ — the output transforms in lockstep with the input.
:::

For the rigid motions relevant here, let the encoder act on the coordinate
matrix $\mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}$ (rows $\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}$), and
let a rotation $\mathbf{R} \in SO(3)$ and translation $\mathbf{t} \in
\mathbb{R}^3$ act by $\mathbf{P} \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{1}_N
\mathbf{t}^{\top}$, where $\mathbf{1}_N \in \mathbb{R}^N$ is the all-ones column
vector. A **scalar** encoder is invariant when

$$ f\!\left(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{1}_N \mathbf{t}^{\top}\right) = f(\mathbf{P}) \qquad \text{(invariance)} $$ {#eq-ch06-invariance}

and a **coordinate-valued** encoder is equivariant when

$$ f\!\left(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{1}_N \mathbf{t}^{\top}\right) = \mathbf{R}\, f(\mathbf{P}) + \mathbf{1}_N \mathbf{t}^{\top} \qquad \text{(equivariance)}. $$ {#eq-ch06-equivariance}

A node-wise equivariant vector field $\mathbf{v}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is the
special case $\mathbf{v}_i(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{1}_N\mathbf{t}^{\top})
= \mathbf{R}\,\mathbf{v}_i(\mathbf{P})$; a node-wise invariant embedding
$\mathbf{h}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ satisfies
$\mathbf{h}_i(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{1}_N\mathbf{t}^{\top}) =
\mathbf{h}_i(\mathbf{P})$.

Equivariant vector features are turned into invariant scalars by taking norms
and inner products: for vectors $\mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{v}_j \in \mathbb{R}^3$
that transform as $\mathbf{v} \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{v}$,

$$ \lVert \mathbf{R}\mathbf{v}_i \rVert_2 = \lVert \mathbf{v}_i \rVert_2, \qquad \langle \mathbf{R}\mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{R}\mathbf{v}_j \rangle = \langle \mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{v}_j \rangle $$ {#eq-ch06-invariant-scalarization}

since $\mathbf{R}^{\top}\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}$. This **scalarization** is what
lets a network mix rotation-sensitive directions into rotation-invariant
descriptors without ever having to align two coordinate frames.

Three symmetries matter here. **Translation** invariance means absolute position
is irrelevant; only relative geometry counts. **Rotation** (and reflection)
invariance means the embedding does not depend on how the molecule is oriented in
the frame. **Permutation** invariance means the result does not depend on the
arbitrary order in which atoms or residues are listed — a set, not a sequence.
A fourth, weaker requirement is often imposed for sequence-conditioned tasks:
the representation should be *equivariant* under a residue reordering only to the
extent that the underlying graph is relabelled with it.

## What each architecture guarantees

@tbl-equivariance states, for the methods discussed below, which symmetries
hold by construction and how they are obtained. The pattern is consistent:
invariant scalar embeddings come from distances and angles, while equivariant
vector or coordinate outputs come from explicitly geometric updates.

| Method | Representation | Rotation | Translation | Permutation | Mechanism |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| GVP-GNN [@jing2021learning] | scalar + vector channels | invariant scalars / equivariant vectors | invariant | invariant | geometric vector perceptron separates scalar and vector features |
| EGNN [@satorras2021n] | node scalars + coordinates | equivariant | invariant | invariant | updates coordinates from weighted relative differences |
| GearNet [@zhang2023protein] | residue graph, distance edges | invariant | invariant | invariant | edge features are distances/angles only |
| ProteinMPNN [@dauparas2022robust] | backbone graph, orientations | invariant | invariant | invariant (decoder order fixed) | relative distances and frames |
| AlphaFold2 [@jumper2021highly] | MSA + pair + frames | equivariant coordinates | invariant | invariant | invariant point attention over local frames |
| ESM-IF [@hsu2022learning] | backbone coordinate graph | invariant | invariant | invariant | GVP-style encoder over backbone |
| TM-vec [@hamamsy2022tmvec] | one vector per structure | invariant | invariant | invariant (set of residues) | supervised by TM-align superposition |

: Invariance and equivariance properties of representative protein structure
encoders. "Invariant" means the output does not change; "equivariant" means it
changes with the input transformation. All methods are invariant to permutation
of the input ordering (@eq-ch06-permutation-invariance). {#tbl-equivariance}

Each entry in @tbl-equivariance is an instance of (@eq-ch06-invariance)
or (@eq-ch06-equivariance). Scalar-only encoders (**GearNet**, **TM-vec**) build every
feature from invariant quantities — pairwise distances and bond/dihedral angles —
so their outputs are invariant by (@eq-ch06-invariant-scalarization).
GVP-style encoders split features into an invariant scalar channel and an
equivariant vector channel, with the vector channel transforming as
$\mathbf{V} \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{V}$ (@eq-ch06-gvp); **ESM-IF** uses
this over backbone geometry. **EGNN** propagates coordinates through
(@eq-ch06-egnn-update), giving translation-invariant, rotation-equivariant
node coordinates. **ProteinMPNN** and **AlphaFold2** are best described by the
*conditional* form: their predicted sequence likelihood
(@eq-ch06-inverse-folding) and their output coordinates are functions of
rotation-invariant features, so a global rigid motion leaves the likelihood
unchanged and rotates the predicted coordinates in lockstep. In every case the
guarantee is a consequence of *what the features are* — invariant scalars versus
equivariant vectors — not of an architectural trick applied afterward.

# Graph Neural Networks and Geometric Methods

## GVP-GNN

The Geometric Vector Perceptron (GVP) network [@jing2021learning] represents each
residue node with two parallel channels: scalar features (invariant) and vector
features (equivariant). Write a GVP input as a pair $(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{V})$
with $\mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{\nu \times
3}$ (each of the $\nu$ rows a 3-vector). A GVP layer produces
$(\mathbf{s}', \mathbf{V}')$ by

$$ \mathbf{s}' = \mathrm{ReLU}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_m \mathbf{s} + \mathbf{b}\right), \qquad \mathbf{V}' = \sigma^{+}\!\left(\mathbf{W}_\mu \mathbf{s} + \mathbf{b}'\right) \odot \left(\mathbf{W}_\nu \mathbf{V}\right) $$ {#eq-ch06-gvp}

where $\mathbf{W}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$,
$\mathbf{W}_\mu \in \mathbb{R}^{\mu \times n}$, and
$\mathbf{W}_\nu \in \mathbb{R}^{\mu \times \nu}$ are learned weights, $\mathrm{ReLU}$ is
the element-wise activation, $\sigma^{+}$ is a sigmoid gate producing values in
$(0,1)^{\mu}$, and $\odot$ broadcasts that gate over the $\mu$ rows of
$\mathbf{W}_\nu \mathbf{V}$ (a Hadamard product). The map
$\mathbf{W}_\nu \mathbf{V}$ is applied row-wise, so each output row is a linear
combination of input 3-vectors. Under a rotation of the input vector channel
$\mathbf{V} \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{V}$ (every row rotated) the gate is
unchanged, because it depends only on the invariant scalars $\mathbf{s}$, and
linearity gives $\mathbf{W}_\nu(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{V}) =
\mathbf{R}(\mathbf{W}_\nu\mathbf{V})$; hence $\mathbf{V}' \mapsto
\mathbf{R}\mathbf{V}'$, i.e. the vector channel is equivariant by
(@eq-ch06-equivariance) and the scalar channel invariant. Keeping most
parameters in the scalar channel is what makes GVP models compact, while the
vector channel carries exactly the rotation-sensitive information. The form shown
in @eq-ch06-gvp is a simplified exposition of the GVP: the full layer of Jing et
al. (2021) also scales the vector channel by a normalisation term computed from
the row-wise vector norms $\lVert\mathbf{V}\rVert_2$, which we omit here for
clarity [@jing2021learning].

## EGNN

The E(n) Equivariant Graph Neural Network [@satorras2021n] achieves equivariance
without higher-order tensors. Let $\mathbf{h}_i^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ be the
node scalar feature and $\mathbf{x}_i^{(l)} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ the node coordinate
at layer $l$. Each layer forms an edge message from invariant quantities,

$$ \mathbf{m}_{ij} = \phi_e\!\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(l)}, \mathbf{h}_j^{(l)}, \lVert \mathbf{x}_i^{(l)} - \mathbf{x}_j^{(l)} \rVert_2^2, a_{ij}\right) $$ {#eq-ch06-egnn-message}

with $\phi_e$ a learned function and $a_{ij}$ optional edge attributes, then
updates coordinates and features,

$$ \mathbf{x}_i^{(l+1)} = \mathbf{x}_i^{(l)} + c \sum_{j \neq i} \left(\mathbf{x}_i^{(l)} - \mathbf{x}_j^{(l)}\right) \phi_x(\mathbf{m}_{ij}), \qquad \mathbf{h}_i^{(l+1)} = \phi_h\!\left(\mathbf{h}_i^{(l)}, \sum_{j \neq i} \mathbf{m}_{ij}\right) $$ {#eq-ch06-egnn-update}

where $\phi_x$ maps the message of (@eq-ch06-egnn-message) to a scalar weight
and $c$ is a normalization constant (for example $c = 1/(N-1)$). The weight
$\phi_x(\mathbf{m}_{ij})$ depends on coordinates only through the invariant
distance $\lVert \mathbf{x}_i^{(l)} - \mathbf{x}_j^{(l)} \rVert_2^2$, and the
displacement $(\mathbf{x}_i^{(l)} - \mathbf{x}_j^{(l)})$ is a difference of
coordinates, so translation cancels. Substituting the rigid motion
$\mathbf{x}_i^{(l)} \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}_i^{(l)} + \mathbf{t}$ therefore
gives $\mathbf{x}_i^{(l+1)} \mapsto \mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}_i^{(l+1)} +
\mathbf{t}$: the coordinate update is translation-invariant and
rotation-equivariant, and the scalar features are invariant (@eq-ch06-invariance). EGNN needs no higher-order tensor features and has become a
default geometry-aware backbone.

## GearNet

GearNet [@zhang2023protein] is a residue-level graph network that combines
sequence edges, radius edges in 3D, and $k$-nearest-neighbor edges, with edge
features restricted to distances and angles,

$$ \mathbf{e}_{ij} = \left(\lVert \mathbf{x}_i - \mathbf{x}_j \rVert_2,\ \theta_{ijk}, \dots\right) $$ {#eq-ch06-gearnet-edge}

where $\theta_{ijk}$ denotes a bond angle at a shared neighbor $k$. Every
component of (@eq-ch06-gearnet-edge) is invariant under a rigid motion —
distances by (@eq-ch06-distance-invariance), angles by
(@eq-ch06-invariant-scalarization) — so the whole encoder is invariant by
(@eq-ch06-invariance). Its emphasis is on **self-supervised pretraining**:
multitask objectives such as masked residue prediction, distance and dihedral
prediction, and contrastive learning across structure views. The result is a
general-purpose structural representation that transfers to residue- and
protein-level prediction tasks.

## ProteinMPNN

ProteinMPNN [@dauparas2022robust] is a message-passing network for **inverse
folding** — predicting an amino-acid sequence that folds into a given backbone.
Given the backbone graph $\mathcal{G}$ with coordinates $\mathbf{P}$, the model
defines a conditional distribution over sequences
$\mathbf{a} = (a_1, \dots, a_N) \in \mathcal{A}^N$, where $\mathcal{A}$ is the
20-letter amino-acid alphabet ($|\mathcal{A}| = 20$), and is trained by teacher
forcing to maximize the likelihood of the native sequence,

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IF}}(\theta) = -\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi \sim \mathrm{Unif}(S_N)}\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{N} \log p_\theta\!\left(a_{\pi(i)} \mid a_{\pi(<i)}, \mathcal{G}\right)\right] $$ {#eq-ch06-inverse-folding}

where $\pi \in S_N$ is a decoding order drawn uniformly from the $N!$
permutations, $a_{\pi(<i)} = (a_{\pi(1)}, \dots, a_{\pi(i-1)})$ is the
already-decoded prefix, and $\theta$ collects the encoder and decoder
parameters. The only geometric inputs to $p_\theta$ are invariant features —
distances between backbone atoms and relative frames — so the likelihood inherits
rotation and translation invariance,
$p_\theta(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{R}\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{1}_N\mathbf{t}^{\top})
= p_\theta(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{P})$ (@eq-ch06-invariance), and
randomizing $\pi$ makes training order-agnostic. Despite its modest size it is a
strong baseline [@dauparas2022robust], and its sequence-design success is direct
evidence that a compact, geometry-aware embedding captures the chemistry of
folding well enough to invert it.

# Structure as a Teacher

The most influential structures are now *predicted* rather than experimental.
Prediction models expose internal representations that are themselves useful
embeddings, and predicted structures serve as a vast training corpus.

## AlphaFold2 and ESMFold representations

AlphaFold2 [@jumper2021highly] represents a protein through an Evoformer over the
multiple sequence alignment and a pair representation, then a structure module
that applies **invariant point attention** to produce 3D coordinates. The
structure module outputs coordinates $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i$ that are equivariant to
a global rigid motion,
$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i(\{\mathbf{R}\mathbf{x}_j + \mathbf{t}\}) =
\mathbf{R}\,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_i(\{\mathbf{x}_j\}) + \mathbf{t}$
(@eq-ch06-equivariance), while the single and pair representations are
invariant; invariant point attention enforces this by weighting points through
invariant distances expressed in local frames. The single and pair
representations that precede the coordinates are rich summaries of sequence and
co-evolutionary context, and they have been reused as features for downstream
tasks. ESMFold [@lin2023evolutionary] removes the MSA requirement: it feeds
embeddings from a large protein language model directly into a folding module,
showing that the structure-relevant information already present in a sequence
embedding can be decoded into coordinates without an explicit alignment.

## Inverse folding and ESM-IF

Inverse folding inverts the classical problem: given a backbone, what sequence
fits it? ESM-IF [@hsu2022learning] trains a GVP-based encoder over the backbone
together with an autoregressive sequence decoder on millions of AlphaFold-predicted
structures. Its GVP encoder follows (@eq-ch06-gvp), so the backbone embedding
is invariant to global rigid motion. The encoder's hidden states are a structure
embedding learned under a strong, self-supervised-style signal (the sequence that
generated the structure), and the model transfers to mutation-effect and
sequence-design tasks. This is the clearest example of **structure as a
teacher**: predicted structures provide the supervision that turns geometry into
a transferable representation.

# Fold Embeddings

A second family of methods does not embed residues or atoms at all; it assigns a
single vector to an entire structure or fold, optimizing for retrieval.

## TM-vector

TM-vec [@hamamsy2022tmvec] learns one vector per protein structure for fast
homology detection and alignment. Its supervision derives from structural
alignment quality — the TM-score produced by TM-align [@zhang2005tmalign] — so
that structurally similar proteins land close together in the embedding space
even when their sequences have diverged beyond recognition. Because the TM-score
is computed after optimal superposition, the training signal carries no
orientation information, and the encoder consumes invariant structural features;
the learned per-structure vector is therefore invariant to rotation and
translation (@tbl-equivariance). This deliberately targets the
regime where sequence search fails, and the resulting vectors support approximate
nearest-neighbor search over databases of millions of structures. TM-score and
related superposition metrics are therefore both the evaluation target and the
training signal.

## Structural alphabets

An alternative to real-valued embeddings is **discretization**. Foldseek
[@vankempen2023foldseek] converts each residue's local backbone geometry into a
small alphabet of structural states (3Di), turning a structure into a string over
an alphabet of a few tens of symbols. That string is then searched with the same
fast sequence-alignment machinery used for amino-acid sequences. Discretization
trades resolution for speed and interoperability: one can index billions of
structures with mature sequence-search infrastructure. The trade-off mirrors the
fingerprint-versus-learned-embedding choice of Chapter 7 — compact and fast
versus expressive and slow — and both are often used together, with the alphabet
as a prefilter and a learned embedding or alignment as the reranker.

# Linking Sequence and Structure Embeddings

Sequence and structure embeddings are two views of one object, and the most
useful representations exploit that relationship. Protein language models trained
on sequence alone already encode structural information: probes of ESM-1b
recover secondary structure and even residue contacts [@rives2021biological], and
ESMFold shows that such embeddings can be decoded into coordinates
[@lin2023evolutionary]. Conversely, structure-trained encoders such as ESM-IF
and GearNet transfer to sequence-level and functional tasks
[@hsu2022learning; @zhang2023protein].

Two practical consequences follow. First, alignment between the two views can be
learned explicitly: a model can be trained so that the sequence embedding of a
protein and the structure embedding of the same protein are close, which is a
contrastive, multimodal objective in the sense of Chapter 9. Second, because
sequence embeddings are cheap and structure embeddings are expensive, a common
recipe is to *distill* structure knowledge into a sequence model, obtaining
structure-aware sequence embeddings at inference time without running a folding
model. The open question throughout is what each view uniquely contributes:
sequence embeddings carry evolutionary and mutational signal, structure
embeddings carry the geometric constraints that evolution actually selected for,
and neither is a complete substitute for the other [@zhang2023protein].

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key Takeaways
- A structure embedding must be translation- and rotation-invariant, and
  permutation-invariant; distance, angle, and frame features enforce this, while
  raw coordinates do not.
- Geometric networks split the problem into invariant scalars and equivariant
  vectors or coordinates: GVP [@jing2021learning] gates vector channels,
  EGNN [@satorras2021n] updates relative coordinates, and AlphaFold2
  [@jumper2021highly] uses invariant point attention on local frames.
- Residue-graph encoders (GearNet [@zhang2023protein]) and inverse-folding models
  (ProteinMPNN [@dauparas2022robust], ESM-IF [@hsu2022learning]) are the
  workhorses for transferable per-residue and per-protein representations.
- Predicted structures have become the training corpus: ESMFold
  [@lin2023evolutionary] and the millions of AlphaFold models behind ESM-IF show
  that geometry can be learned at scale without waiting for experimental data.
- Whole-fold embeddings range from continuous vectors, optimized against
  alignment scores (TM-vec [@hamamsy2022tmvec]), to discrete structural
  alphabets for fast search (Foldseek [@vankempen2023foldseek]).
- Sequence and structure embeddings are complementary; probes
  [@rives2021biological] and cross-view transfers are most effective when the two
  are linked rather than treated as rivals.
:::
